note: Real human hardware left on the Moon outside the south polar region (the polar relics live in relics.json). lat/lon are planetocentric, east-positive. Positions: NASA/LROC and the Wikipedia 'List of artificial objects on the Moon' (which cites them).

coords_source.name: List of artificial objects on the Moon

sites.title: Apollo 11 - Tranquility Base
left: Plaque: We came in peace for all mankind
facts: Armstrong and Aldrin spent 21 h 36 min on the surface on 20-21 July 1969, with one moonwalk of about 2 h 31 min.
The laser reflector they placed is still used: observatories on Earth time laser echoes to measure the Moon's distance to the millimeter.
The ascent engine blast knocked the flag over; the descent stage still stands as the launch pad.
sites.nasa_q: Apollo 11 Tranquility Base lunar module descent stage LRO
sites.serp_q: Apollo 11 landing site Tranquility Base what was left on the Moon

sites.title: Apollo 12 - Ocean of Storms
left: ALSEP science station with a nuclear power unit
facts: Conrad and Bean landed about 155 m from the Surveyor 3 probe, a precision landing that proved Apollo could target a spot.
They cut off Surveyor 3's camera and parts and brought them home to study how materials aged on the Moon.
Their ALSEP was the first to run on a radioisotope generator and sent data until 1977.
sites.serp_q: Apollo 12 landing site Surveyor 3 Intrepid ALSEP left on the Moon

sites.title: Apollo 14 - Fra Mauro
facts: Shepard and Mitchell climbed toward Cone crater hauling a two-wheeled equipment cart nicknamed the lunar rickshaw.
At the end Shepard hit two golf balls with a makeshift 6-iron head.
They returned 42 kg of rock from the Fra Mauro formation, ejecta from the Imbrium impact.
sites.nasa_q: Apollo 14 Fra Mauro Antares Shepard Mitchell
sites.serp_q: Apollo 14 landing site Fra Mauro what was left on the Moon golf balls

sites.title: Apollo 15 - Hadley Rille
facts: Scott and Irwin drove the first Lunar Roving Vehicle about 28 km over three moonwalks beside the Hadley Rille canyon.
Their retroreflector has 300 prisms, three times larger than the Apollo 11 and 14 arrays, and is the most used by ranging stations.
They left a small aluminum figure, Fallen Astronaut, with a plaque naming astronauts and cosmonauts who died in the space race.
sites.nasa_q: Apollo 15 Hadley Rille lunar rover Scott Irwin
sites.serp_q: Apollo 15 landing site Hadley Rille lunar rover left on the Moon Fallen Astronaut

sites.title: Apollo 16 - Descartes Highlands
facts: Young and Duke were the first to land in the lunar highlands, expecting volcanic rock; the samples turned out to be impact breccias.
They brought back 95 kg of samples and drove the rover about 27 km.
Duke left a photo of his family on the surface; it is still there, bleached by sunlight.
sites.nasa_q: Apollo 16 Descartes Young Duke lunar rover
sites.serp_q: Apollo 16 landing site Descartes highlands what was left on the Moon

sites.title: Apollo 17 - Taurus-Littrow
left: Plaque: Here man completed his first explorations of the Moon
facts: Cernan and Schmitt, a geologist, were the last humans on the Moon, leaving on 14 December 1972.
They drove about 36 km, the farthest of any crew, and found orange volcanic glass soil at Shorty crater.
They returned 110 kg of samples, the most of any mission.
sites.nasa_q: Apollo 17 Taurus-Littrow Cernan Schmitt orange soil
sites.serp_q: Apollo 17 landing site Taurus-Littrow what was left on the Moon

sites.title: Surveyor 1
facts: On 2 June 1966 it made the first US soft landing on the Moon, proving the ground could carry a spacecraft.
It sent back more than 11,000 pictures before the lunar night ended its mission.
sites.serp_q: Surveyor 1 first US soft landing Moon 1966

sites.title: Surveyor 3
left: Surveyor lander (camera and parts were taken home by Apollo 12)
facts: Apollo 12's crew walked to it in November 1969 and cut off the TV camera and other parts for study on Earth.
It is the only spacecraft on the Moon that humans have visited.
sites.serp_q: Surveyor 3 Apollo 12 crew visited camera returned

sites.title: Surveyor 5
facts: Its alpha-scattering instrument made the first chemical analysis of lunar soil on the spot, showing it was basalt-like.
It landed in Mare Tranquillitatis, near where Apollo 11 would land two years later.
sites.serp_q: Surveyor 5 alpha scattering lunar soil analysis

sites.title: Surveyor 6
left: Surveyor lander (moved 2.4 m from its first spot)
facts: On 17 November 1967 it fired its engines for 2.5 seconds, lifted about 4 m and landed 2.4 m away, the first liftoff from another world.
The hop let engineers photograph its own landing footprints and measure the soil.
sites.serp_q: Surveyor 6 first liftoff from the Moon hop

sites.title: Surveyor 7
facts: The last Surveyor landed in the highlands beside Tycho crater in January 1968.
Two laser beams fired from Earth were seen by its camera, the first lasers detected on the Moon.
sites.serp_q: Surveyor 7 Tycho laser beams detected from Earth

sites.title: Luna 9
facts: On 3 February 1966 it made the first soft landing on the Moon and sent the first pictures from the surface.
Its landing proved the surface was solid enough for a lander, not deep dust.
sites.nasa_q: Luna 9 Soviet first soft landing Moon
sites.serp_q: Luna 9 first soft landing on the Moon 1966

sites.title: Lunokhod 1
facts: The first remote-controlled rover on another world drove 10.5 km over 11 months, steered by a crew on Earth.
LRO photographed it in 2010 and a laser echo from its reflector was received that April, after decades of being lost.
sites.serp_q: Lunokhod 1 rover found by LRO 2010 retroreflector laser

sites.title: Lunokhod 2
facts: It drove about 39 km in four months in Le Monnier crater, a distance record for another world that stood for decades.
It stopped after the lid fell on dust-covered radiators and overheated it.
sites.serp_q: Lunokhod 2 Le Monnier crater 39 km record rover

sites.title: Luna 16
left: Descent stage (the return capsule brought 101 g of soil to Earth)
facts: In September 1970 it drilled into Mare Fecunditatis and returned 101 g of soil, the first robotic sample return from another world.
sites.serp_q: Luna 16 first robotic sample return Moon 1970

sites.title: Luna 24
left: Descent stage (the return capsule brought 170 g of core to Earth)
facts: The last Soviet lunar mission drilled a 2 m core in Mare Crisium and returned 170 g of it in August 1976.
After it, no spacecraft softly landed on the Moon for 37 years until Chang'e 3.
sites.serp_q: Luna 24 Mare Crisium drill core sample return 1976

sites.title: Chang'e 3 and Yutu
facts: On 14 December 2013 China made the first soft landing on the Moon in 37 years, in Mare Imbrium.
Yutu's ground-penetrating radar found distinct layers of lava flows beneath the surface.
sites.serp_q: Chang'e 3 Yutu rover Mare Imbrium radar layers

sites.title: Chang'e 4 and Yutu-2
facts: On 3 January 2019 it made the first soft landing on the far side of the Moon, in Von Karman crater, with a relay satellite to reach Earth.
Yutu-2 has driven for years, longer than any earlier lunar rover, and found unusual mantle-like rock.
sites.nasa_q: Chang'e 4 far side Von Karman LRO
sites.serp_q: Chang'e 4 far side landing Von Karman crater Yutu-2 results

sites.title: Chang'e 5
left: Lander (the ascender took 1.7 kg of samples home)
facts: In December 2020 it returned 1,731 g of the youngest lunar rock yet, from lava about 2 billion years old.
It was the first lunar sample return since Luna 24 in 1976.
sites.nasa_q: Chang'e 5 landing site LRO Mons Rumker
sites.serp_q: Chang'e 5 sample return youngest lunar basalt 2 billion years

sites.title: Chang'e 6
left: Lander (the ascender took 1.9 kg of far-side samples home)
facts: In June 2024 it brought back the first samples from the far side of the Moon, from Apollo basin inside the South Pole-Aitken basin.
sites.nasa_q: Chang'e 6 landing site LRO Apollo basin far side
sites.serp_q: Chang'e 6 far side sample return Apollo basin results

sites.title: SLIM
left: Two small probes, LEV-1 and LEV-2
facts: On 19 January 2024 Japan's lander came down within about 55 m of its target, a pinpoint landing near Shioli crater.
It tipped onto its nose and its solar cells faced the wrong way, yet it worked for days and woke up again after lunar nights.
sites.nasa_q: SLIM lander Japan Moon LRO image
sites.serp_q: SLIM JAXA lander pinpoint landing nose down Shioli crater
